overview: The SQL LIKE operator performs pattern matching on text using two wildcards: `%` matches any sequence of zero or more characters, and `_` matches exactly one character.

An optional ESCAPE clause lets you match literal `%` or `_` characters, and case sensitivity depends on the column/database collation (with ILIKE offering explicit case-insensitive matching in some engines).
A leading-wildcard pattern like `'%term'` cannot use a normal B-tree index, forcing a full scan — a key performance consideration for search features.
learningObjectives: Use the `%` (any sequence) and `_` (single character) wildcards correctly to build LIKE patterns.
Apply the ESCAPE clause to match literal `%` and `_`, and understand case sensitivity, collation, and ILIKE.
Explain why leading-wildcard LIKE prevents normal index usage and what alternatives exist for substring search.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: LIKE is a SQL predicate of the form `expr LIKE pattern [ESCAPE escape_char]` that returns TRUE when the string expr matches the pattern. Within the pattern, `%` matches any substring (including empty), and `_` matches any single character; all other characters match literally. An ESCAPE character designates the following `%`, `_`, or escape character itself as a literal. Matching uses the effective collation, which determines case and accent sensitivity. NOT LIKE negates the result, and NULL operands yield UNKNOWN (the row is excluded).
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: LIKE is fuzzy text search with two wildcards. `%` is a placeholder for 'anything, any length' and `_` is a placeholder for 'exactly one character'. So `'A%'` finds anything starting with A, `'%son'` finds anything ending in son, `'%log%'` finds anything containing log, and `'_at'` finds three-letter words ending in 'at' like cat, bat, hat. If you actually want to find a real percent sign, you use ESCAPE to say 'this % is literal, not a wildcard'.
coreConcept.historicalContext: LIKE has been in SQL since SQL-86 and is supported by every major relational database. The `%` and `_` wildcards and the ESCAPE clause are standardized. Vendors added extensions: PostgreSQL's ILIKE for case-insensitive matching, SIMILAR TO and regex operators (~) for richer patterns, and trigram (pg_trgm) and full-text indexes to overcome LIKE's leading-wildcard performance limitation that became painful as text search scaled.

whyItMatters.business: Pattern search powers product search bars, customer lookup by partial name, log filtering, and data-quality rules (e.g., emails matching a domain). Correct, fast LIKE behavior directly affects user experience and operational efficiency.
whyItMatters.engineering: LIKE is the simplest portable text-matching tool, but engineers must understand wildcard semantics, escaping, collation-driven case sensitivity, and the indexability rules to avoid correctness bugs and runaway full scans.
whyItMatters.scalability: Leading-wildcard LIKE forces full scans that do not scale; recognizing this drives the adoption of trigram indexes, full-text search, or external engines as data volume grows.
whyItMatters.cost: A `'%term%'` query over a large table scans every row, inflating CPU/IO and cloud scan costs; choosing the right index or search strategy keeps text queries affordable.
whyItMatters.reliability: Knowing that case sensitivity is collation-dependent and that special characters must be escaped prevents intermittent, environment-specific matching bugs that are hard to reproduce.

coreComponents.name: Percent Wildcard (%)
coreComponents.definition: Matches any sequence of zero or more characters within the pattern.
coreComponents.purpose: Enables prefix, suffix, and substring matching of variable length.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Placed at the start (suffix match), end (prefix match), or both (contains match); a leading % defeats normal index use.

coreComponents.name: Underscore Wildcard (_)
coreComponents.purpose: Matches fixed-length patterns or single-position variation.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Each `_` consumes exactly one character — no more, no fewer; combine multiple for fixed-length masks.
coreComponents.examples: '_at' (cat, bat, hat), 'A__' (A followed by exactly two chars), '2024-__-__' (date mask)

coreComponents.name: ESCAPE Clause
coreComponents.definition: Designates a character that makes the following %, _, or escape character itself match literally.
coreComponents.purpose: Allows searching for actual percent signs or underscores in the data.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Defines a single escape character; the pattern must escape every literal wildcard occurrence consistently.
coreComponents.examples: WHERE code LIKE '50\%%' ESCAPE '\' finds codes starting with '50%'

internalWorking: The matcher walks the pattern left to right: literal characters must match the input exactly (subject to collation), `_` consumes one input character, and `%` allows the matcher to skip any number of characters (a backtracking match).
When an ESCAPE character is defined, the matcher treats the immediately following %, _, or escape char as a literal rather than a wildcard.

The optimizer inspects the pattern: an anchored prefix (no leading wildcard, e.g. `'abc%'`) can be converted into a range scan on a B-tree index, while a leading `%` or `_` makes the predicate non-sargable, forcing a full scan or a specialized text index.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Parser (pattern + ESCAPE) -> Optimizer (anchored prefix => index range scan; leading wildcard => full scan / trigram / FTS) -> Storage Engine (scan & match per row, collation-aware) -> Result Set
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A query runs `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email LIKE 'admin%';`.
2. The optimizer sees the pattern is anchored at the start (prefix match) and an index exists on email.
3. It performs an index range scan over emails from 'admin' up to the next prefix boundary.
4. Each candidate is collation-compared to confirm the prefix; matching rows are returned. Had the pattern been `'%admin'`, the optimizer would fall back to a full table scan.

keyTerminology.meaning: A special pattern character (% or _) that matches characters in the input rather than itself.
keyTerminology.importance: The core mechanism of LIKE; misusing % vs _ produces wrong matches.

keyTerminology.meaning: A pattern with literal characters at the start before any wildcard, e.g. 'abc%'.
keyTerminology.importance: Only anchored-prefix LIKE can use a normal B-tree index as a range scan.

keyTerminology.meaning: Rules governing string comparison, including case and accent sensitivity and sort order.
keyTerminology.importance: Determines whether LIKE is case-sensitive; the same query can match differently across databases due to collation.

keyTerminology.meaning: A predicate the optimizer can satisfy via an index seek/range scan.
keyTerminology.importance: Anchored LIKE is sargable; leading-wildcard LIKE is not, which dictates performance.

importantConcepts.concept: Why leading-wildcard LIKE can't use a normal index
importantConcepts.explanation: A B-tree index is ordered by the start of the string. A pattern like `'%abc'` or `'%abc%'` has no known prefix, so the engine cannot seek to a starting point and scan a contiguous range — it must inspect every row (full scan). Only patterns anchored at the start (`'abc%'`) translate to a range scan. To make substring/suffix search fast, use a trigram index (PostgreSQL pg_trgm), full-text search, a reversed-string index (for suffix search), or an external search engine.

Whether `'a%'` matches 'Apple' depends on collation. PostgreSQL's default collation is case-SENSITIVE, so LIKE is case-sensitive; ILIKE provides case-insensitive matching. MySQL's default collations (e.g. utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci) are case-INSENSITIVE, so LIKE ignores case there. SQL Server depends on the column/database collation (CI vs CS). For portable case-insensitive matching, normalize with LOWER(col) LIKE LOWER(pattern) (note: this can break index usage) or use a case-insensitive collation/ILIKE.

variationsAndTypes: **Prefix match (`'abc%'`):** Anchored, sargable, index-friendly — the fastest LIKE form.
**Suffix match (`'%abc'`):** Leading wildcard, non-sargable; needs a reversed-string index or full scan.
**Contains match (`'%abc%'`):** Leading and trailing wildcard; needs trigram/full-text index to be fast.
**ILIKE / case-insensitive LIKE:** Explicit case-insensitive matching (PostgreSQL ILIKE) or via case-insensitive collation.
advantages: **Simple and portable:** Standard wildcard syntax works across all major databases.
**Readable patterns:** % and _ express common prefix/suffix/contains/mask searches concisely.
**Index-friendly when anchored:** Prefix patterns use B-tree range scans efficiently.
**ESCAPE support:** Cleanly matches literal % and _ characters.
disadvantages: **Leading-wildcard full scans:** `'%x'` and `'%x%'` cannot use a normal index and scale poorly.
**Collation-dependent case behavior:** The same pattern matches differently across databases, causing portability bugs.
**Limited expressiveness:** No alternation, quantifiers, or character classes — that requires regex/SIMILAR TO.
**Escaping burden:** Literal % and _ in data require careful ESCAPE handling to avoid wrong matches.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use LIKE for simple prefix searches (`'abc%'`), fixed-length masks with `_`, and low-volume or indexed substring lookups where a portable, readable predicate is sufficient.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid plain LIKE for high-volume substring/suffix search (`'%x%'`, `'%x'`) on large tables — use trigram indexes, full-text search, or a dedicated search engine instead; avoid relying on implicit case behavior across databases.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: LIKE is like searching a phone book. Looking up everyone whose surname starts with 'Mc' (`'Mc%'`) is fast — you flip straight to that section because the book is ordered by the start of the name. But finding everyone whose surname CONTAINS 'son' (`'%son%'`) means reading every single entry cover to cover, because the alphabetical ordering gives you no shortcut. That is exactly why a leading wildcard can't use the index.

commonMisconceptions.myth: LIKE is always case-insensitive (or always case-sensitive).
commonMisconceptions.reality: Case behavior depends entirely on collation. PostgreSQL LIKE is case-sensitive by default; MySQL's default collations make it case-insensitive. Never assume — check the collation or use ILIKE / explicit LOWER().

commonMisconceptions.myth: Adding an index makes any LIKE query fast.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only anchored-prefix patterns (`'abc%'`) use a normal B-tree index. Leading-wildcard patterns (`'%abc'`, `'%abc%'`) still require a full scan unless you use a trigram or full-text index.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Anchored-prefix LIKE scales via index range scans; leading-wildcard search does not. At scale, migrate substring/suffix search to trigram (pg_trgm) or full-text indexes, or offload to a search engine like Elasticsearch.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Collation-driven case sensitivity is the top reliability risk; pin collations explicitly and test matching behavior per environment. Escape user-supplied wildcards to keep results correct.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: LIKE is deterministic given the same data and collation; ensure consistent collation across replicas and restores so matching behavior does not drift.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Watch for slow queries with leading-wildcard LIKE in the plan (sequential/full scans) and alert on text-search latency regressions.
productionConsiderations.security: Treat user search input as untrusted: parameterize it AND escape % and _ in the input so users cannot inject unintended wildcards (a denial-of-service or over-broad-match risk) or SQL.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Replacing `'%term%'` full scans with trigram/full-text indexes drastically cuts scanned bytes and CPU, lowering cost in pay-per-scan and high-QPS systems.
productionConsiderations.performance: Keep the column bare for anchored patterns to preserve index usage; avoid wrapping it in LOWER() unless backed by a functional/expression index or case-insensitive collation.

codeExamples.title: The % and _ wildcards: prefix, suffix, contains, and fixed-length masks
codeExamples.overview: Demonstrates every common LIKE pattern using % (any sequence) and _ (single character), plus NOT LIKE.
codeExamples.breakdown: `%` stands for any run of characters (including none), so 'John%' matches 'John' and 'Johnny'; '%@gmail.com' matches any address ending in that domain; '%error%' matches the substring anywhere. `_` matches exactly one character, so '_at' matches 'cat'/'bat' but not 'at' or 'chat', and '___' matches strings of exactly three characters. NOT LIKE returns the complement (and, like LIKE, excludes NULLs).
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Prefix returns John, Johnny, etc.; suffix returns all gmail addresses; contains returns log lines mentioning error; '_at' returns 3-letter ...at words; '___' returns 3-character codes; NOT LIKE returns everyone not starting with John.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Confusing `_` (one char) with `%` (any length); forgetting that `'John%'` also matches exactly 'John'; assuming `%error%` uses an index (it does not).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Anchor patterns at the start (`'John%'`) so a B-tree index range scan applies; for `'%error%'` use a trigram or full-text index instead of plain LIKE.

codeExamples.title: ESCAPE clause for literal % and _, plus case-insensitive matching
codeExamples.overview: Shows how to match literal percent/underscore characters using ESCAPE, and how to do case-insensitive matching via ILIKE or LOWER().
codeExamples.breakdown: With `ESCAPE '\'`, the sequence `\%` means a literal percent sign, so `'50\%%'` reads as: literal '50%' followed by a wildcard `%` (anything after). `'A\_B'` matches the exact text A_B because `\_` is a literal underscore, not a single-char wildcard. ILIKE is PostgreSQL's case-insensitive LIKE. `LOWER(name) LIKE LOWER(...)` is portable but wrapping the column in LOWER() can prevent a normal index from being used unless an expression index on LOWER(name) exists.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: The first query returns codes literally beginning with '50%'; the second returns rows where sku is exactly 'A_B'; ILIKE and the LOWER form both match Apple/APPLE/apple.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting the ESCAPE clause so % is treated as a wildcard; choosing an escape char that also appears in the data; LOWER() silently disabling index usage; assuming ILIKE exists in all databases (it is PostgreSQL-specific).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: For frequent case-insensitive prefix search, create an expression index on LOWER(name) or use a case-insensitive collation so the predicate stays index-friendly.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: An e-commerce site has a product search bar. Engineers implemented it as `name LIKE '%:term%'`. As the catalog grew to millions of rows, search latency climbed to seconds, and case-sensitivity differences between the staging (PostgreSQL) and a legacy MySQL service produced inconsistent results.
endToEndExample.inputData: A `products` table with name (TEXT), sku (VARCHAR), and a B-tree index on name. Search terms are arbitrary user-typed substrings, sometimes containing % or _ characters.
endToEndExample.architecture: PostgreSQL primary with read replicas. Search queries originate from the storefront and must be both fast and case-insensitive.
processingSteps: 1. Diagnose slowness: EXPLAIN shows a sequential (full) scan because the leading `%` makes the pattern non-sargable.
2. Address case sensitivity: switch the user-facing match to ILIKE (PostgreSQL) so 'iphone' matches 'iPhone'.
3. Sanitize input: escape user-supplied % and _ with an ESCAPE clause so a search for '50%' does not act as a wildcard.
4. Enable substring performance: create a pg_trgm GIN index on name so `name ILIKE '%term%'` uses the trigram index instead of a full scan.
5. Re-test latency and verify identical, case-insensitive results across environments by pinning collation.
endToEndExample.output: A fast, case-insensitive product search that returns correct matches for arbitrary substrings, treats user-typed % and _ as literals, and uses a trigram index instead of scanning every row.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Track p95 search latency and the fraction of search queries doing sequential scans; alert if trigram index usage drops or latency regresses.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Validate and escape search input; cap pattern length and reject pathological patterns. Return an empty, well-formed result for blank searches rather than a wildcard-everything scan.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Search latency drops from seconds to milliseconds via the trigram index, results are consistently case-insensitive across databases, and user-entered wildcard characters are handled as literals — a robust, scalable search feature built on LIKE/ILIKE done correctly.

industryUseCases.problem: Letting shoppers find products by partial, case-insensitive name or SKU substrings at scale.
industryUseCases.solution: Use anchored LIKE/ILIKE for prefix autocomplete and trigram (pg_trgm) or full-text indexes for `%term%` substring search, escaping user-entered wildcards.
industryUseCases.benefits: Fast, relevant, case-insensitive search that scales beyond what plain leading-wildcard LIKE could handle.

industryUseCases.problem: Filtering log lines that contain specific keywords or error patterns.
industryUseCases.solution: Use LIKE '%error%' for ad-hoc filters on smaller windows and dedicated full-text/inverted indexes for high-volume search, with collation pinned for consistency.
industryUseCases.benefits: Flexible keyword filtering with a clear migration path from LIKE to indexed search as volume grows.

industryUseCases.problem: Agents searching customers by partial name, email domain, or ticket reference, including literal special characters.
industryUseCases.solution: Use prefix LIKE for indexed name lookups, suffix matching on email domains, and ESCAPE to handle literal % or _ in references; ILIKE/collation for case-insensitivity.
industryUseCases.benefits: Accurate, forgiving customer lookups that handle special characters and case variations correctly.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Anchored-prefix LIKE scales with B-tree range scans; substring/suffix search does not. Scale it with pg_trgm GIN/GiST indexes, full-text (tsvector) indexes, reversed-column indexes for suffix search, or an external engine like Elasticsearch.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Matching is deterministic given identical data and collation. Pin collation across primary, replicas, and restored backups so LIKE/ILIKE behavior does not silently diverge after failover or recovery.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: LIKE evaluates identically on replicas; route search-heavy read traffic to replicas. Ensure trigram/full-text indexes are replicated and built consistently across nodes.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Results depend only on data, pattern, and collation, so restores reproduce matches; verify that collation settings and text-search indexes are restored alongside the data.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Anchor patterns to enable index range scans; add pg_trgm for `%x%`, expression indexes on LOWER(col) for case-insensitive prefix search, and full-text indexes for tokenized search. Inspect EXPLAIN to confirm index (not sequential) scans.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Eliminating leading-wildcard full scans via trigram/full-text indexes cuts CPU, IO, and scanned bytes — major savings in high-QPS or pay-per-scan environments.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Parameterize search input and additionally escape % and _ within the value so users cannot inject unintended wildcards (over-broad matches / ReDoS-like scans) or SQL. Bound pattern length.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Alert on queries showing sequential scans for LIKE predicates and on rising text-search latency; track trigram/full-text index hit rates.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Validate that stored text uses a consistent collation and encoding; test that escaping handles literal % and _ in data, and that case behavior matches expectations per environment.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log slow LIKE queries with their plans; alert when a search predicate degrades from index scan to full scan, indicating a missing or unused text index.

recommendedPractices: **Anchor patterns when possible:** Prefer `'abc%'` so a B-tree index range scan applies; avoid leading wildcards on large tables.
**Use trigram/full-text indexes for substring search:** For `'%x%'` and `'%x'`, back the query with pg_trgm or full-text indexes rather than relying on LIKE alone.
**Escape user-supplied wildcards:** Escape % and _ in user input with an ESCAPE clause so searches match literally.
**Be explicit about case:** Use ILIKE, a case-insensitive collation, or an expression index on LOWER(col) rather than relying on implicit behavior.
engineeringStandards: Forbid unbounded leading-wildcard LIKE on large tables in code review unless backed by a trigram/full-text index.
Always parameterize and wildcard-escape user search input to prevent injection and accidental wildcards.
Pin and document column/database collation so case and accent sensitivity are explicit and portable.
designRecommendations: Design search features with the indexing strategy chosen up front (prefix index vs trigram vs full-text) based on expected query shapes.
Store a normalized (e.g., lowercased) copy or use an expression index when case-insensitive prefix search is common.
For suffix search, consider storing and indexing a reversed copy of the column.
namingConventions: Name expression indexes by the expression, e.g. `idx_users_lower_email`.
documentationStandards: Document the collation and case-sensitivity assumptions for each searchable column.
Note which LIKE patterns are index-backed and which intentionally fall back to scans.
Record the chosen ESCAPE character convention for handling literal wildcards.
testingStrategies: Test % vs _ semantics explicitly (e.g., '_at' must not match 'at' or 'chat').
Test ESCAPE handling with data containing literal % and _ characters.
Test case sensitivity across target databases/collations and verify EXPLAIN uses the expected index for anchored patterns.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using leading-wildcard LIKE (`'%term%'`) on a large table and expecting it to be fast.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Developers add an index on the column and assume any LIKE will use it.
commonMistakes.impact: The query performs a full table scan because the leading % has no prefix to seek on, causing severe latency at scale.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Anchor the pattern when possible, or use a trigram (pg_trgm) or full-text index for substring/suffix search; offload to a search engine for heavy workloads.

commonMistakes.mistake: Not escaping user-supplied % and _ in search input.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Input is concatenated or bound directly into the pattern without sanitizing wildcard characters.
commonMistakes.impact: A user searching for '100%' or 'order_id' triggers unintended wildcard matches (over-broad results) and can cause expensive scans; concatenation also risks SQL injection.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Parameterize the value AND escape % and _ within it using an ESCAPE clause, so the input matches as literal text.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming LIKE has the same case sensitivity everywhere.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Code developed on a case-insensitive MySQL collation is moved to case-sensitive PostgreSQL (or vice versa).
commonMistakes.impact: Searches that worked in one environment silently miss results in another, producing hard-to-reproduce, environment-specific bugs.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Be explicit: use ILIKE or a case-insensitive collation for case-insensitive matching, or LOWER(col) LIKE LOWER(pattern) backed by an expression index; pin collations.

comparisonSection.explanation: `=` tests exact equality and is fully index-sargable. LIKE adds wildcard pattern matching (% and _). Use `=` when you want exact matches (it is faster and clearer); use LIKE only when you genuinely need wildcards. A LIKE with no wildcards behaves like `=` but signals intent less clearly.

Anchored-prefix LIKE is sargable and uses a B-tree index range scan, scaling well. Leading-wildcard LIKE is non-sargable and forces a full scan because the index ordering gives no starting point — it requires a trigram or full-text index to be fast.

LIKE does literal substring matching with no language awareness and scans rows without a special index. Full-text search tokenizes text, supports stemming, ranking, and stop-words, and is backed by inverted indexes — far better for natural-language search at scale, at the cost of more setup and less literal precision.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between the % and _ wildcards in LIKE?
beginnerQuestions.answer: `%` matches any sequence of zero or more characters, while `_` matches exactly one character. So `'a%'` matches any string starting with 'a' of any length, and `'a_'` matches a two-character string starting with 'a'. `'_at'` matches three-letter words like cat and bat but not 'at' or 'chat'.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: The single most common LIKE question. State both wildcards precisely and give a contrasting example showing _ is exactly one character.

beginnerQuestions.question: How do you search for a literal percent sign or underscore with LIKE?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Use the ESCAPE clause to designate an escape character, then prefix the literal % or _ with it. For example, `WHERE code LIKE '50\%%' ESCAPE '\'` matches codes starting with the literal text '50%'. The `\%` is a literal percent, while the trailing `%` is still a wildcard.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Show you know ESCAPE exists and how it disambiguates literal wildcard characters. Mention you can choose any escape character.

intermediateQuestions.question: Why can't a query like `WHERE name LIKE '%smith'` use a normal index?
intermediateQuestions.answer: A B-tree index is ordered by the beginning of the string. A leading wildcard means the start of the value is unknown, so the engine has no prefix to seek to and cannot scan a contiguous range — it must examine every row (a full scan). Only anchored-prefix patterns like `'smith%'` can use a B-tree range scan. To make suffix/substring search fast, use a trigram index, a reversed-column index, or full-text search.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Explain index ordering and sargability, then offer concrete fast alternatives (trigram/reversed index/FTS).

intermediateQuestions.question: Is LIKE case-sensitive? How do you do case-insensitive matching?
intermediateQuestions.answer: It depends on collation. PostgreSQL LIKE is case-sensitive by default; MySQL's default collations are case-insensitive. For explicit case-insensitive matching use ILIKE in PostgreSQL, a case-insensitive collation, or `LOWER(col) LIKE LOWER(pattern)` (which may bypass a plain index unless an expression index on LOWER(col) exists).
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Emphasize collation-dependence and give portable techniques. Note the index trade-off of LOWER().

advancedQuestions.question: A `%term%` search on a 50M-row table is slow. Walk through how you'd make it fast.
advancedQuestions.answer: EXPLAIN will show a sequential scan because the leading wildcard is non-sargable. Options: (1) if a prefix suffices, anchor it as `'term%'` to use a B-tree range scan; (2) for true substring search, create a pg_trgm GIN/GiST index so `LIKE '%term%'` uses trigram matching; (3) for natural-language search, move to full-text (tsvector) with a GIN index; (4) for very large/high-QPS workloads, offload to a dedicated search engine like Elasticsearch. Also escape user wildcards and pin collation.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Demonstrate the diagnosis (EXPLAIN, sargability) and a tiered set of solutions from cheap (anchor) to heavy (external engine).

advancedQuestions.question: How would you safely handle user-supplied search text in a LIKE query?
advancedQuestions.answer: Bind the value as a parameter to prevent SQL injection, then escape the wildcard characters % and _ within the value (e.g., replace `%` with `\%`, `_` with `\_`) and apply an ESCAPE clause, so user-typed wildcards are treated as literals. Optionally cap length and reject pathological inputs to avoid expensive scans.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Cover both injection (parameterization) and the subtler wildcard-injection issue (escaping % and _), plus DoS bounding.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A support tool searches customers with `LOWER(name) LIKE LOWER('%' || :q || '%')`. It works but is slow, and a search for 'a&b_co' returns too many rows. Diagnose and fix.
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Two issues: performance and correctness. The leading % plus LOWER() prevents normal index use, and the unescaped underscore in 'a&b_co' acts as a single-char wildcard, over-matching. Fix by escaping user wildcards, and improve performance with a trigram index (optionally on LOWER(name)) or a case-insensitive collation.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Escape % and _ in the user term and add an ESCAPE clause so 'a&b_co' matches literally. For speed, add a pg_trgm index (and/or an expression index/collation for case-insensitivity) so the substring search uses an index instead of scanning. Verify with EXPLAIN that the trigram index is used.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design the search backend for a product catalog supporting prefix autocomplete and full substring search over tens of millions of items, case-insensitively.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Use anchored LIKE/ILIKE on an indexed (or expression-indexed lowercase) name column for fast prefix autocomplete. For substring search, add a pg_trgm GIN index so `ILIKE '%term%'` is index-backed, or push to a full-text/Elasticsearch tier for ranking and language features. Escape user wildcards and pin collation.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Prefix LIKE is cheap and index-friendly but limited to prefixes; trigram indexes enable substring search at the cost of index size and write overhead; full-text/Elasticsearch add ranking and language awareness but more infrastructure and eventual-consistency considerations.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Serve autocomplete from indexed prefix queries on replicas; route heavy substring/ranked search to trigram-indexed tables or a dedicated search cluster; cache popular queries. Bound and sanitize input to prevent expensive scans.

How would you make a suffix search (`'%abc'`) fast?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: LIKE matches text against a pattern where % means any sequence of characters and _ means exactly one character.
keyConcepts: % = any sequence (0+ chars); _ = exactly one char.
Case sensitivity depends on collation; ILIKE = case-insensitive (PostgreSQL).
Anchored prefix 'abc%' uses an index; leading '%abc' forces a full scan.
Use trigram/full-text indexes for fast substring search.
formulas: '%' matches any substring (incl. empty); '_' matches exactly one character
commands: SELECT * FROM t WHERE name LIKE 'John%';
SELECT * FROM t WHERE word LIKE '_at';
SELECT * FROM t WHERE code LIKE '50\%%' ESCAPE '\';
SELECT * FROM t WHERE name ILIKE 'apple%';
interviewPoints: Leading wildcard '%x' can't use a normal index -> full scan.
Case sensitivity is collation-dependent; use ILIKE/LOWER().
For '%x%' use trigram or full-text indexes.
quickNotes: ESCAPE '\' makes \% a literal percent sign.
PostgreSQL LIKE is case-sensitive; MySQL default collations are not.
Escape user-typed % and _ to avoid unintended wildcards and over-broad matches.

keyTakeaways: LIKE pattern-matches text with two wildcards: `%` matches any sequence of zero or more characters and `_` matches exactly one character.
Use the ESCAPE clause to match literal % or _ (e.g., `LIKE '50\%%' ESCAPE '\'`), and always escape user-supplied wildcards to avoid over-broad matches and injection.

Case sensitivity is collation-dependent (PostgreSQL LIKE is case-sensitive, MySQL's defaults are not); use ILIKE, a case-insensitive collation, or LOWER() for explicit, portable case-insensitive matching.

A leading-wildcard pattern like `'%abc'` or `'%abc%'` cannot use a normal B-tree index and forces a full scan, because the index is ordered by the start of the string; only anchored prefixes (`'abc%'`) are index-friendly.
For fast substring/suffix search at scale, move beyond plain LIKE to trigram (pg_trgm), full-text indexes, reversed-column indexes, or a dedicated search engine.
